strengths: Significance of Benchmark Contribution: The paper introduces the SceneDiff Benchmark, which is the first instance-level multiview object change detection dataset featuring distinct camera trajectories between 'before' and 'after' sequences. The dataset is diverse (350 video pairs across 50 scenes, combining handheld captures and egocentric sequences from HD-Epic) and densely annotated with instance masks, change categories, and deformability.

Well-Conceived Scene-Centric Metric: Beyond conventional pixel-level and view-level metrics, the proposed obj/sc AP appropriately evaluates whether detected changes across multiple frames and trajectories correspond to consistent 3D physical object instances, which is critical for real-world downstream tasks.

Sound Training-Free Method Design: The SceneDiff framework combines foundation models (pi^3, DINOv3, SAM) into an effective pipeline. Key design choices—such as the asymmetric depth reprojection test to separate occlusion from removal/addition, combining pixelwise reprojected feature comparison with region-level pooled matching, and voxel-based 3D consistency aggregation—are well reasoned and systematically ablated.

Extensive Evaluation and Generalization: The method significantly outperforms existing approaches (including CYWS, 3DGS-CD, and VLM baselines) on both the new benchmark and established datasets (RC-3D, PASLCD, ChangeSim). The robotics demonstration (tidy-up task with a 7-DoF manipulator) further confirms the practical utility of the proposed representation.

Thorough Analysis and Transparent Limitations: The supplementary material provides extensive ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, runtime profiling, failure mode analyses (e.g., repetitive textures, extreme lighting shifts), and detailed baseline adaptations.
weaknesses: Algorithmic Novelty: The method primarily functions as a modular system integration combining off-the-shelf foundation models (feed-forward geometry regressor pi^3, visual representation DINOv3, segmenter SAM) alongside an association procedure closely inspired by ConceptGraph. While the combination is thoughtful and well-tuned, the core algorithmic innovation is incremental.

Sensitivity to Upstream Geometry Failure: As analyzed in Section 7.5, SceneDiff strictly depends on the accuracy of the multi-view geometry regression. In challenging cases involving sparse overlaps, textureless surfaces, or repetitive patterns, registration failure directly cascades into total detection failure.

Computational Efficiency: The pipeline takes ~160 seconds per sequence pair on an NVIDIA A40 GPU, largely dominated by SAM generating whole- and part-level masks across all candidate frames. This currently limits online or interactive robotic use-cases without further optimization or lighter backbone choices.

strengths: Important and well-formulated benchmark: The proposed SceneDiff Benchmark addresses a significant gap in visual change detection by introducing 350 real-world video pairs captured along disparate camera trajectories with dense, instance-level annotations and explicit 'added/removed/moved' semantics.

Comprehensive and multi-level evaluation metrics: Introducing obj/sc AP alongside traditional pixel-level IoU and view-level AP effectively evaluates scene-centric physical object consistency across views rather than just isolated 2D predictions.

Sound, training-free algorithmic design: The proposed SceneDiff algorithm effectively orchestrates 3D foundation models (pi^3), segmentation (SAM), and semantic features (DINOv3). The asymmetric geometric reprojection formulation and multi-cue scoring scheme (E_geom, E_feat, E_region) are technically well motivated.

Extensive experimental validation and ablations: The method achieves clear improvements over existing 2D/3D baselines on both the new benchmark and established datasets (RC-3D, PASLCD, ChangeSim). The paper also provides detailed ablations of geometry backbones, feature representations, and hyperparameter sensitivity.
Practical robotic demonstration: The real-world closed-loop robotic tidying application provides a compelling demonstration of how multiview change detection can directly guide physical interaction.
weaknesses: High computational latency: Processing a single sequence pair takes ~160 seconds (Table 9), primarily driven by generating SAM whole and part masks across all frames, which presents a bottleneck for interactive or real-time robotic systems.

Sensitivity to upstream foundation model failures: The pipeline is multi-stage (feed-forward 3D reconstruction -> SAM masking -> feature extraction -> voxel aggregation -> greedy association), making it susceptible to error compounding if the geometry model fails under sparse overlap or if SAM segments incorrect object boundaries.

Limitations in repetitive and ambiguous environments: As noted in the failure analysis, scenes with dense, repetitive items (e.g., supermarket shelves) degrade both the appearance matching and region association stages, leading to severe performance drops.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem in 3D spatial understanding: instance-level object change detection across differing camera trajectories and viewpoints, moving beyond traditional near-duplicate viewpoint assumptions.

Valuable benchmark contribution (SceneDiff Benchmark): provides 350 diverse video sequence pairs (200 newly collected in varied indoor/outdoor environments and 150 from HD-Epic) with dense, temporally consistent instance-level annotations across frames, significantly expanding beyond prior small-scale multiview datasets like PASLCD (20 sequences) and 3DGS-CD (5 sequences).

Sound and effective training-free formulation: the integration of feed-forward 3D geometry estimation, asymmetric depth difference reasoning to disambiguate occlusion from absence, SAM-based object regioning, and DINOv3 feature matching is technically sensible and domain-general.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation and strong results: significantly outperforms 2D/3D correspondence methods (CYWS), 3DGS-based render-and-compare methods, and VLM baselines on both the new benchmark and existing benchmarks (RC-3D, PASLCD, ChangeSim).

Thorough ablation studies and practical grounding: provides clear ablations over geometry backbones and visual cues, transparent failure mode analysis, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, and a real-world closed-loop robotic tidying demonstration.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is relatively incremental: the method is primarily an assembly and heuristic integration of existing pretrained foundation models (feed-forward geometry models such as π³, SAM, DINOv3, and ConceptGraph-style 3D clustering) rather than introducing fundamentally new learning paradigms or core representations.

Heavy reliance on the performance of feed-forward geometry regressors: the ablation in Table 5 and failure analysis show that the method's efficacy drops severely when using alternative geometry backbones (e.g., FASt3R or VGGT) or under low visual overlap and extreme lighting changes, where initial co-registration fails.

Inference latency: at approximately 160 seconds per sequence pair (as reported in Table 9), the multi-stage pipeline is computationally heavy, primarily due to dense multi-view SAM prompting/mask generation and multi-model feature unprojection, which may limit real-time interactive robotic deployments.

Dataset scale in terms of physical environments: while 350 sequence pairs is larger than previous multiview change datasets, they stem from 50 physical scenes, and a notable portion (150 pairs) is sampled from kitchen activities in HD-Epic, which somewhat concentrates the scene variety.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging open problem: detecting object-level changes (added, removed, moved) between unconstrained multi-view video captures taken at different times with significant viewpoint shifts.

The proposed SceneDiff Benchmark is a valuable community contribution: 350 video pairs across diverse indoor/outdoor scenes and egocentric cooking activities (HD-Epic) with dense, frame-level instance segmentation annotations, filling a clear gap compared to small-scale or semantic-only prior datasets.

The training-free method is well-engineered to tackle key geometric challenges, specifically using directional visibility masking to handle occlusions versus actual scene changes, multi-cue scoring (geometry, reprojected DINO features, and region matching), and 3D voxel aggregation.

Extensive experimental validation and ablations across multiple geometry foundation models (pi^3, VGGT, FASt3R) and feature backbones, demonstrating large gains over existing methods (CYWS-3D, 3DGS-CD, and VLM baselines) alongside a physical robot tidying demonstration.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is moderate: the framework is largely an integration of several existing foundation models (pi^3, SAM, SAM 2, DINOv3) combined with heuristic thresholds and score weighting rather than a new learned model or representation.

Strong dependency on feed-forward 3D reconstruction: the entire pipeline relies on joint geometry estimation across both sequences; when changes are substantial or overlap is low, the geometry backbone can fail or invert static vs. dynamic elements (as shown in Fig. 13 and 15).
Evaluation metric leniency: the point-based evaluation allows up to two prediction points per ground-truth bounding box without penalty, which could potentially mask over-segmentation issues.

High inference latency: processing a sequence pair requires ~159 seconds on an NVIDIA A40 GPU (primarily due to dense per-frame SAM prompting), which hinders real-time robotics deployment without significant optimization.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem in 3D vision and spatial understanding: detecting object-level additions, removals, and movements across multi-view video sequences captured under varying viewpoints.

Introduces SceneDiff Benchmark, the first dense instance-level multi-view change detection dataset spanning 350 diverse video pairs (both varied daily indoor/outdoor scenes and egocentric cooking scenes from HD-Epic), accompanied by an efficient SAM2-based annotation pipeline and evaluation protocols.

Proposes a well-motivated, training-free approach that effectively coordinates feed-forward 3D geometry estimation (pi^3), semantic feature comparison (DINOv3), and instance segmentation (SAM). The asymmetric geometric reprojection rule cleanly separates viewpoint-dependent occlusions from genuine additions/removals.

Achieves convincing performance gains over baselines (CYWS-3D, 3DGS-CD, and VLM + Grounding SAM) on the proposed benchmark, while also establishing new state-of-the-art results on existing two-view benchmarks (RC-3D, ChangeSim).

Extensive ablations and qualitative analyses provide clear insights into component contributions (appearance vs. geometry, choice of 3D backbone, feature extractors) and failure modes (repetitive objects, severe lighting shifts, large camera displacement).
Demonstrates practical real-world utility through an end-to-end table-tidying robotic manipulation setup.
weaknesses: High computational cost: As reported in Table 6, inference requires ~160 seconds per sequence pair, driven largely by per-frame multi-granularity SAM mask extraction, which presents a bottleneck for interactive or real-time robotic systems.

Heuristic point-based evaluation metric: The evaluation protocol relies on mapping predictions to centroids and ground truth to bounding boxes, permitting up to two prediction points per GT object without penalty. While motivated by part-whole segmentation ambiguity, it relaxes spatial localization precision compared to standard mask or bounding-box IoU thresholds.

Performance drop on complex egocentric data: Detection performance degrades considerably on the egocentric Kitchen subset (SD-K, dropping to 20.9 AP compared to 46.3 AP on SD-V), underscoring that heavy clutter, deformable items, and rapid head motion remain substantial challenges for the pipeline.

Vulnerability to underlying model failure modes: The system is inherently sensitive to joint geometry regression failures; if the initial multi-view alignment fails due to limited scene overlap or widespread simultaneous object displacements, downstream scoring and association fail entirely.

strengths: Significance of the Benchmark: The paper introduces the SceneDiff Benchmark, filling a critical gap in the literature. While prior benchmarks either assume fixed/near-duplicate viewpoints, lack instance-level annotations, or only cover two views with single changes, SceneDiff offers 350 diverse video pairs (both varied daily scenes and egocentric cooking scenes) with dense, instance-level annotations across visible frames.

Sound and Effective Training-Free Pipeline: The proposed SceneDiff method effectively leverages modern visual foundation models (π³ for 3D reconstruction, SAM for instance proposals, and DINOv3 for semantic representations). The design choices—such as the asymmetric depth difference rule to handle occlusions, the combination of reprojected and region-level appearance matching, and 3D voxelized score aggregation—are well-motivated and technically sound.

Substantial Empirical Superiority: SceneDiff significantly outperforms existing baselines (e.g., 3DGS-CD, CYWS-3D, and VLM baselines) across per-view and per-scene metrics on the proposed benchmark, while also achieving state-of-the-art results on existing datasets including RC-3D and ChangeSim.

Thorough Analysis and Ablations: The paper provides extensive ablations analyzing the contribution of each score component, the influence of different geometry backbones (π³ vs. VGGT vs. FASt3R), feature representations, sensitivity to thresholds, and transparently details failure modes (such as scenes with identical repetitive items and reconstruction failures).
Real-World Embodied Demonstration: The authors successfully demonstrate the practical utility of SceneDiff in a physical robotic tidying application using a 7-DoF manipulator arm.
weaknesses: Sensitivity to Upstream Geometry: As an uncalibrated multiview framework relying on feed-forward geometry estimation (π³), the change detection accuracy is inherently capped by the quality of 3D reconstruction and camera alignment. When sequences have low overlap or extreme perspective differences, failure in joint geometry leads to complete failure in change detection.

Computational Latency: The runtime is relatively high (~159 seconds per sequence pair), largely dominated by generating both part- and whole-object masks with SAM across multiple views, which could limit time-sensitive or real-time robotic deployments.

Multi-Stage Heuristics: The pipeline contains several hand-crafted hyperparameters and thresholds (e.g., co-visibility cutoff of 50%, τ_occ, combination weights λ_g, λ_f, λ_r, σ_geo, σ_merge, and τ_sim). Although sensitivity studies in the supplementary show reasonable stability, the multi-stage heuristic composition could require tuning when moving to completely different camera distributions or sensor modalities.
